Instead you juice them into a bright green, grassy, slightly sweet drink and take it as a small shot. Growing it is quick and always the same: soak the wheat berries, spread them thickly on a shallow tray, cover the tray to keep it dark for a couple of days, then move it into the light and cut the grass near the base in about a week to ten days. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so it grows the same wherever you live. The main thing to watch is mold, since the crowded, damp seed mat can grow it easily, so spread the seeds evenly, keep air moving, and do not soak them too long.
seasoned: Wheatgrass is the young shoot of common wheat (Triticum aestivum), grown indoors and harvested as a grass rather than eaten as a leaf. Unlike salad microgreens, the fibrous blades are too tough to chew, so wheatgrass is pressed into a fresh, intensely green, grassy-sweet juice and taken as a shot. The cycle is short and repeatable: soak the wheat berries, spread them in a dense even mat on a shallow tray, give a brief dark blackout, then light to green up, and cut near the base at the jointing stage in about 7 to 10 days. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a counter anywhere. The one real challenge is mold: the dense wet seed mat is prone to it, so an even sow, steady airflow, and not over-soaking are the whole craft.

beginner: Your wheatgrass is ready when the blades are about 6 to 7 inches tall and a second blade is just starting to appear, usually 7 to 10 days after planting. Cut it near the base with clean scissors and juice it right away. It does not grow back well, so you start a fresh tray each time.
seasoned: Cut wheatgrass at the jointing stage, when a second blade just begins to split from the first, usually at about 6 to 7 inches and 7 to 10 days from sowing. Snip near the base with clean scissors and juice it fresh. The mat will not give a strong second cut, so each tray is a single harvest.
